 Jerusalem Post / Israel Election 2026 Former police spokesman slams election day arrests, accuses commissioner, police of major failures
 Former police spokesman Eli Levy accused senior officers of relying on unverified intelligence in election day arrests and criticized the police commissioner's silence.
 Follow us on Google Israel Police Commissioner Insp. Gen. Daniel Levy casts his ballot in the 26th Knesset election, October 27, 2026. ( photo credit : ISRAEL POLICE SPOKESPERSON'S UNIT ) By 103FM NOVEMBER 17, 2026 12:59 Former police spokesman Cmdr. (ret.) Eli Levy sharply criticized the Israel Police over arrests carried out on election day, accusing senior officers of failing to verify intelligence and Police Commissioner Insp.-Gen. Danny Levy of remaining silent amid the controversy, in an interview with Gideon Oko and Amichai Attali on 103FM on Tuesday.
 The controversy surrounding the election day arrests, along with an unusual statement by Police Commissioner Danny Levy suggesting that the Prime Minister's Office may have deceived the police , has drawn sharp criticism from former senior police officials.
 Speaking on Tuesday morning, Eli Levy, a former police spokesman, criticized the decision-making process at the highest levels of the organization and the commissioner's failure to communicate with the public.
 Levy expressed full support for Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara 's decision to freeze the police's internal investigation after the commissioner sought to appoint his deputy to lead it.
 "The attorney-general is unequivocally right," Levy said. "Police Commissioner Danny Levy made a mistake in deciding to appoint the man whose office is three and a half steps away from his. They eat lunch together most days of the week and are close friends. The police should have appointed an external investigative team made up of retired senior officers acceptable to all sides."
 Gali Baharav-Miara. (credit: YONATAN SINDEL/FLASH90) According to the former police spokesman, the handling of the affair exposed a series of unusual failures in police procedures.
 Prime Minister's Office request bypassed National Security Minister's Office, contrary to procedure 
 Levy pointed out that the request from the Prime Minister's Office was made directly to the police commissioner's aide, bypassing the National Security Minister's Office, contrary to required procedure.
 "This incident is even more unusual because several people were bypassed here. The minister's office was bypassed, but far more seriously, the attorney-general and the State Attorney's Office were bypassed," he said.
 He added: "I'm telling you from experience, I was the police spokesman during much more turbulent years, and there wasn't a single occasion when personnel from the Israel Police's Investigations Division, the Investigations and Intelligence Division, did not consult very senior people both in the State Attorney's Office and in the attorney-general's office."
 More seriously, according to Levy, the decision was made to carry out arrests without consulting the attorney-general or state attorney and without examining the reliability of the intelligence source.
 "None of the police personnel personally met the informant before the arrests," Levy claimed, citing conversations he had held over the previous 24 hours with current and former investigations and intelligence officers.
 "You cannot carry out arrests of this kind based on a single piece of intelligence that has not been cross-checked, and before evidence has been collected. If there is no evidence, you do not make an arrest, and certainly do not issue a statement to the media that shakes up the entire election day."
 Levy also addressed Police Commissioner Danny Levy's statement that "we may have been deceived."
 "This is a far more dramatic event than a quote, something that should resonate in every home in Israel," he said. "The police's job is to ensure that no one succeeds in deceiving them, certainly not on election day."
 Levy says police commissioner's decision not to appear on camera a "terrible mistake" 
 Finally, Levy strongly criticized the police commissioner's decision not to appear before the cameras to provide explanations to the public.
 "This is a terrible mistake. If I were the police spokesman, I would put him in front of a camera to deliver an address to the nation. The police have an excellent public information apparatus and excellent officers who know how to communicate these matters. Every minute that passes without answers, public trust in the police falls to an unprecedented low. This is a dramatic incident that disgraces the police and also seriously damages the police's image."
